problem: Large VLMs give good social reasoning for robot navigation but cannot run on edge robots, while lightweight VLMs lack social reasoning. Standard on-policy distillation uses reverse KL (mode-seeking, unstable on high-entropy teacher outputs) and applies loss uniformly to all tokens, so routine-motion tokens dominate the gradient.
motivation: Social navigation needs human-aware decisions such as yielding and bypassing groups, but deployment on resource-constrained platforms requires small models. Most navigation trajectories consist of low-entropy routine motion where teacher and student already agree, which dilutes supervision on socially critical decisions.
key_idea: Do on-policy distillation from a frozen SFT teacher VLM to a small student VLM using temperature-scaled JSD, applied only on tokens where teacher entropy exceeds a threshold.
insight: Both components matter and are complementary. On MUSON, JSD alone gives Acc 0.893 and the entropy filter alone 0.836 (SFT 0.811), while both together give 0.953. Swapping the divergence for reverse KL (0.885), forward KL (0.853) or weighted JSD (0.861) is clearly worse than temperature JSD (0.953), so temperature control is important.
method: On-policy sampling: the student Qwen2.5-VL-3B autoregressively generates responses from its own policy given image and prompt, so supervision matches its deployment state distribution.
SFT teacher: Qwen3-VL-8B is supervised fine-tuned on the social navigation data and then frozen to provide token-level distributions over student-generated responses.
Temperature scaling: teacher and student logits are softened by softmax(z/lambda) with lambda=2.0.
JSD objective: minimizes Jensen-Shannon divergence between softened teacher and student distributions, following the weighted JSD formulation of GKD/OPD, instead of reverse KL.

Entropy-based token selection: computes teacher entropy H_i at each decoding step and builds a binary mask m_i = 1[H_i > tau] with tau=1.5. Only selected high-uncertainty tokens contribute to the loss, suppressing gradients from trivial low-entropy tokens.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-3B student (fine-tuned via distillation); Qwen3-VL-8B SFT teacher (frozen)
setting.training_data: SNEI and MUSON social navigation datasets, each randomly split 8:2 into train/test; 5 epochs, lr 1e-5, cosine schedule with warmup 0.1, 8 A100 GPUs
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB image plus text prompt
setting.action_space: discrete textual high-level actions (e.g. move forward, move forward left, move forward right) produced as VLM text output
setting.simulator: none (offline dataset evaluation) plus real robot
setting.privileged: none at test time (teacher used only during training)

numbers.eval_set_note: random 20% held-out test split of SNEI (own 8:2 split, not official)
numbers.extra: own random 8:2 split; metrics are action accuracy and Sentence-BERT cosine similarity for perception and reasoning

numbers.eval_set_note: random 20% held-out test split of MUSON (own 8:2 split, not official)
numbers.extra: own random 8:2 split; metrics are action accuracy and Sentence-BERT cosine similarity

numbers_note: Real-world experiments are qualitative only, apart from inference throughput of 0.984 FPS and 2.74 s end-to-end latency (0.365 FPS) on a Scout Mini. No standard navigation benchmarks (SR/SPL) are reported.
results: SOPD achieves the best results on both SNEI and MUSON, e.g. SNEI Acc 0.889 vs 0.863 for the strongest baseline OPSD (SFT 0.692), and MUSON Acc 0.953 vs 0.932 for SKD. In real-world conversation and queuing scenes it outputs 'move forward left' where SKD and OPSD output 'move forward'.
limitations: Evaluation is offline on random 8:2 splits with action-accuracy and cosine-similarity metrics, with no closed-loop navigation success metrics and only qualitative real-world examples.
Real-world latency is high (2.74 s per sample end-to-end, 0.365 FPS) and involves network communication; the entropy threshold is fixed rather than adaptive.
Only one teacher-student pair (Qwen3-VL-8B to Qwen2.5-VL-3B) and single-frame decisions are studied; longer horizons are left to future work.
